targets.authors: Spranca, M., Minsk, E., & Baron, J.
targets.title: Omission and commission in judgment and choice.
targets.evidence_quote: In a pre-registered experiment (N = 313), we successfully replicated an experiment from Spranca, Minsk, and Baron (1991), considered a classic demonstration of the omission bias, examining generalizability to a between-subject design with extensions examining causality, intent, and regret.
targets.outcome_quote: We conclude a successful replication of the baseline omission bias with slight deviations from the original findings regarding outcome bias.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The stated successful verdict is restricted to baseline omission bias. The authors separately mark outcome-bias comparisons as deviations from the same original; the target therefore has agreement and disagreement rather than an unrestricted overall success verdict.

targets.title: The psychology of preferences.
targets.evidence_quote: The classic action-effect (Kahneman & Tversky, 1982) findings were that actions leading to a negative outcome are regretted more than inactions leading to the same negative outcomes. We added a regret measure to examine whether the action-effect findings would extend to situations of morality involving intended harmful behavior. Our findings were opposite to the expected action-effect omission-commission asymmetry with participants rating omissions as more regretted than commissions (d = 0.18 to 0.26).
targets.outcome_quote: The classic action-effect (Kahneman & Tversky, 1982) findings were that actions leading to a negative outcome are regretted more than inactions leading to the same negative outcomes. We added a regret measure to examine whether the action-effect findings would extend to situations of morality involving intended harmful behavior. targets.outcome_reasoning: The added regret measure explicitly tests generalization of this published action-effect finding to moral scenarios and finds the opposite pattern.

reasoning: New participants re-test Spranca et al. Experiment 1 and also conceptually re-test Kahneman and Tversky’s specific regret asymmetry through the added measure. Citations concerning causality and intent motivate extensions without isolating further specific earlier experiments as targets.
